pattern.top_pattern: Inpatient oncology and immunotherapy episodes are emerging as a distinct cost driver
pattern.what_is_impacting: CA / CT / GA, WI, and CA / IP Med/Surg and ACUTE HOSPITAL
key_driver_codes: Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T-cell and Other Immunotherapies
Chemotherapy without Acute Leukemia as Secondary Diagnosis with CC
pattern.pattern_details: Oncology-related inpatient spend is showing up as a separate business issue, not just as noise inside general acute hospital trend. The biggest signals are CAR-T and other immunotherapies at Yale New Haven, inpatient chemotherapy growth in WI, and smaller chemo-related acute hospital pressure in CA. These episodes typically require separate clinical policy, case management, and reimbursement treatment from standard Med/Surg admissions.
pattern.why_it_matters: High-cost oncology episodes can grow quickly and are governed by different medical policy and contract levers than routine inpatient care.
pattern.recommended_next_step: Trigger an oncology episode review for CAR-T and inpatient chemotherapy admissions, including medical policy adherence, site appropriateness, and reimbursement adequacy for these therapies.
evidence_summary: YALE NEW HAVEN HOSPITAL CAR-T and immunotherapy activity added about $2.6M.
WI inpatient chemotherapy added about $1.6M, with 52 more admissions and roughly +$10.5K paid per admit.
CA EPO acute hospital chemotherapy added about $300K.
The pattern combines both more oncology admissions and higher-intensity oncology episodes.
